items.title: Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why
items.summary: The history of technological progress suggests that as AI spreads, the employment impact will hit women more than men.
items.body: Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her. She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20. The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs. The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.

items.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
items.summary: Penalties are seen as too harsh on motorists who are penalised for parking on private land.
items.body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham. The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped . Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies". Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

items.title: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water
items.summary: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. In an…
items.body: Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control , the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility. One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run. Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

items.title: Frank Elderson: From climate and nature risks to economic resilience and competitiveness
items.body: We are living in a time of profound economic, geopolitical and technological uncertainty. Yet amid all this uncertainty, one thing is clear: climate change and nature degradation will continue to shape our economies and societies, and we will have to deal with the consequences. Climate change and nature degradation are a certainty in an uncertain world. The events of this summer have reminded us of that reality in the most tangible way possible. Taken together, this summer’s events conveyed a simple but powerful message: climate and nature are not external to our economies. They are embedded within them and, increasingly, they are becoming a macroeconomic concern.

items.title: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom
items.summary: Iran-backed Houthi militants have launched repeated volleys of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since a deadly airport attack earlier this month.
items.body: Saudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement . The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured. Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser.

items.summary: Sitharaman identified fuel, fertilizer and access to capital as risks for India’s economy in 2027.
items.body: The high degree of liquidity in India's equity market has provided easier exits to foreign portfolio investors, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. "Because of the ease of liquidity, ease of availability, people are even exiting easily," Sitharaman told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday. However, the fundamentals of the Indian economy are "fine," she said. Since January, India's key benchmark indexes have slipped nearly 12%, as per LSEG data, even though the country's economic growth has been resilient amid trade uncertainty and geopolitical shocks. India has been hit with record outflows by foreign investors from its equity markets. Still, domestic capital continues to flood the market.

items.title: US bans DeepSeek AI from government use as tech tension with China continues
items.summary: DeepSeek is a powerful, popular and relatively inexpensive artificial intelligence model out of China.
items.body: The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models. As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race. While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China. The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment. The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.

items.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
items.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops looted France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings…
items.body: France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country. The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt. The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high. This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.

items.title: China’s export boom creates a difficult bargain for Southeast Asia
items.summary: China’s export machine is accelerating as its domestic economy remains under strain. This comes amid growing trade friction as China’s partners question whether persistent surpluses can coexist with balanced and resilient regional growth. Last month, China’s exports rose 36.3…
items.body: China’s export machine is accelerating as its domestic economy remains under strain. This comes amid growing trade friction as China’s partners question whether persistent surpluses can coexist with balanced and resilient regional growth. Last month, China’s exports rose 36.3 per cent year on year, while shipments to Southeast Asia jumped 52.3 per cent. The trade surplus reached US$133.5 billion, taking the nine-month total to US$938.1 billion. In contrast, retail sales grew just 0.4 per cent in August, according to the latest official figures. For the first eight months, fixed-asset investment dropped 7.2 per cent while property investment plunged 19.9 per cent. Yet industrial production for August rose 5.2 per cent. These figures do not prove that exports alone explain China’s resilience or that every factory is overproducing.

items.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay
items.summary: Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan is accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco.
items.body: The Saudi national accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI 's headquarters was ordered detained without bail pending trial Monday by a San Francisco federal judge who said that there is a "significant" risk he would flee. The order came at a court hearing where Judge Alex Tse sharply questioned the value of an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay the full bail for Abdulrahman Alfozan , 35, who was working for OpenAI as an engineer when he allegedly planted the device in a television on Sept. 28. "It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out," Tse said in the courtroom, as Alfozan and several dozen of his supporters looked on.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, says court filing
items.summary: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
items.body: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing , external in California. US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest. The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial. Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder. The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

items.title: North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns
items.summary: More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies. The…
items.body: North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies. The Unite union said on ⁠Monday that more than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers would take part ⁠in a 24-hour ​strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies. A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms. Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.

items.title: China’s economy grows 4.5% in third quarter, staying on track for annual target
items.summary: China’s economy expanded by 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, keeping it broadly on track to meet this year’s growth target but also maintaining pressure on Beijing to deploy further support to address weak domestic demand. China’s year-on-year economic growth for the first…
items.body: China’s economy expanded by 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, keeping it broadly on track to meet this year’s growth target but also maintaining pressure on Beijing to deploy further support to address weak domestic demand. China’s year-on-year economic growth for the first three quarters of the year came in at 4.6 per cent, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said on Monday. Beijing is targeting gross domestic product growth between 4.5 and 5 per cent this year, down from the “around 5 per cent” goal in previous years. The third-quarter growth was above the 4.41 per cent consensus forecast of economists surveyed by Chinese financial data provider Wind. It picked up pace from the 4.3 per cent expansion recorded during the second quarter, which was the lowest quarterly growth rate reported since the end of 2022.

items.title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop
items.summary: Apple sent invitations for an event next week, calling it "Pro and tell."
items.body: Apple announced a product launch event on Oct. 28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles." The email says "Pro and tell," suggesting the launch will focus on high-end "Pro" devices with powerful homegrown chips. Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall. He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year. It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.

items.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
items.summary: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to idenitify and remove listings linked to looting".
items.body: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France . The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting". Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend. "The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said. Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.

items.title: Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion
items.summary: American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have…
items.body: A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced. Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades. The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship. The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004.

items.title: Hong Kong’s Apec meetings give Beijing a venue to pitch the virtues of its system
items.summary: As Hong Kong hosts the Apec finance ministers’ meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part two, Frank Chen explores how the event could help Beijing pitch its philosophies and urge…
items.body: As Hong Kong hosts the Apec finance ministers’ meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part two, Frank Chen explores how the event could help Beijing pitch its philosophies and urge cooperation in digital infrastructure financing. China’s hosting of this year’s Apec meetings, including a finance ministers’ gathering in Hong Kong, will see a more confident Beijing seek to pitch its economic and financial governance philosophies to other countries, analysts say. That desire – and ambition – to showcase the feats and experience of the world’s second-largest economy to member nations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum was bolstered by perceived “inadequacies” in the ability of Western doctrines to address challenges, they added.

items.title: Anthropic is AI trade's last big hope for a major IPO this year
items.summary: On Kalshi, Anthropic is seen as the last major IPO in 2026 after OpenAI delayed its public market debut. Others have postponed too.
items.body: Heading into 2026, investors were excited at the prospect of a host of new initial public offerings , including ones from mega-cap private companies like SpaceX , Anthropic and OpenAI . But now investors will have to settle for less than they expected at the start of the year, with OpenAI ruling out its debut on the public markets in 2026 and several other planned offerings postponed this year . On prediction market platform Kalshi , speculators think the only major company left that might officially announce an IPO this year is Anthropic, which confidentially filed a prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in early June. The market on Kalshi asks traders if they think a series of companies will officially announce an IPO in 2026.

items.title: Bikes 'not for jousting,' says Lime after duel video
items.summary: Footage emerged on social media of hundreds of people gathered in east London to watch a bike joust.
items.body: E-bike rental company Lime has said its bikes are "not for jousting" after footage of two riders dressed as knights charging at each other in an east London park circulated over the weekend. Hundreds of people congregated in London Fields, Hackney, to watch artist Jack Carden and actor Camtholomew the First joust, while riding the bright green rentable e-bikes. The videos on social media showed them dressed as knights in armour, complete with chainmail and lances, attempting to knock each other off the bikes. A spokesperson for the company said: "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first." Ahead of the event, Carden said the "free public joust" was "performance art" in a post on social media. A video on his Instagram account of the event has been watched more than four million times.

items.title: ‘Concerning issues’ found at GB power grid by inquiry into cover-up claims
items.summary: Neso control room staff accused senior executives of covering up extent of blackout risks during June heatwave Independent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural issues” at Great Britain’s grid operator after control room staff accused senior executives of…
items.body: Independent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural issues” at Great Britain’s grid operator after control room staff accused senior executives of covering up the extent of blackout risks in the UK during the June heatwave. An external legal firm tasked with investigating a series of whistleblower allegations against the National Energy System Operator (Neso) raised concerns over how high levels stress among control room engineers was handled by the company. The three-month investigation began after whistleblowers accused Neso of a cover-up over the growing risk of blackouts . They claimed the grid was becoming increasingly unmanageable, and that control room decisions were subject to “interference” by the company’s corporate affairs team to protect the reputation of the government-owned operator.

items.title: Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year
items.summary: The SpaceX boss said Monday that he'll give one of his company shares to every child in the U.S. next year. He didn't say how the share giveaway would happen.
items.body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company. There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data. That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday. "This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.

items.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
items.summary: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
items.body: Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC. The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations. The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since. One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results. He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price. "Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price.

items.title: Bank of England said to be reviewing Barclays’ handling of private credit loans
items.summary: Concerns financial contracts known as derivatives were incorrectly logged, potentially boosting Barclays’ profits The Bank of England is reportedly looking into Barclays’ handling of loans linked to the embattled private credit sector. The Bank’s regulatory arm, the Prudential…
items.body: The Bank of England is reportedly looking into Barclays’ handling of loans linked to the embattled private credit sector. The Bank’s regulatory arm, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), started reviewing the matter this year after concerns were raised by a Barclays insider, according to the Financial Times. The concerns related to the way Barclays logged the derivatives, known as total return swaps, used to finance the loans it issues to private credit firms. Those derivatives – financial contracts that track the performance of an underlying asset – are said to have been logged in the wrong portfolio, indicating they were less risky than they actually were. That could mean the bank was not holding enough capital to cover potential losses, and could have boosted its profitability.

items.title: Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical
items.summary: Google says its Minnesota AI data center will add clean energy to the grid and protect ratepayers. Experts question whether grid upgrades are needed.
items.body: If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard. A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs. Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use. Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power. Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis.

items.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge public share giveaways
items.summary: Musk's announcement comes after Anthropic pledged to create a public benefit fund ahead of its blockbuster stock market listing.
items.body: Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity. Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year. The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good". Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn. The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.

items.title: Ofcom investigates Huw Edwards complaint over Channel 5 drama
items.summary: Former BBC presenter says programme starring Martin Clunes gave a misleading and unfair account of his downfall Britain’s media regulator is investigating a complaint from the former BBC news presenter Huw Edwards about a Channel 5 drama depicting his downfall. Ofcom said it was…
items.body: Britain’s media regulator is investigating a complaint from the former BBC news presenter Huw Edwards about a Channel 5 drama depicting his downfall. Ofcom said it was investigating Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards , which starred Martin Clunes and was broadcast earlier this year, under its “fairness and privacy” rules. The drama became the channel’s highest-rated show of the year after its broadcast in March, attracting 3.8 million viewers in four weeks. Edwards, once one of the BBC’s highest-paid newsreaders, confirmed to the Guardian that he had made the complaint. He said he had a series of concerns about its depiction of the events that led up to his disgrace. The 65-year-old pleaded guilty to accessing indecent photographs of children in July 2024 and was sentenced to six months in prison, suspended for two years.

items.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
items.summary: The chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee says families should not be taxed through no fault of their own.
items.body: Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned. Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free. Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own. The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman. However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait. The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

items.title: More than half of UK first-time buyers paying more for mortgage than they did for rent
items.summary: Hamptons says figure of 56% is highest in at least a decade, with mortgage rates rising since start of Iran war A majority of first-time UK buyers now pay more towards their monthly mortgage bills than they used to pay in rent, the estate agent Hamptons has found. Last month 56%…
items.body: A majority of first-time UK buyers now pay more towards their monthly mortgage bills than they used to pay in rent, the estate agent Hamptons has found. Last month 56% of first-time buyers said their monthly mortgage bills exceeded their previous rent, the highest proportion in at least a decade, according to Hamptons. They paid £39 more on average. Mortgage rates have been climbing in the UK since the outbreak of war in the Middle East, as volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate deals. Earlier this month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years . On Monday morning the average rate stood at 5.99%, while the average rate for a two-year fixed mortgage was 5.96%, according to the financial analyst Moneyfacts.

items.title: France hit by worst unrest in years as attempts to rein in government spending meet citizen ire
items.summary: France’s worst unrest in years saw thousands arrested, prompting President Macron to vow an “uncompromising” response ahead of a critical budget vote.
items.body: France endured its worst unrest in years this weekend as nationwide protests over high living costs and declining public services turned violent ahead of a key government vote on the budget. Demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with almost 2,400 people arrested, shops looted or damaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country, according to the interior ministry. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, the ministry said.

items.title: China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports
items.summary: Exports have helped offset weak spending at home, but trade tensions and AI doubts cloud its outlook.
items.body: China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports. The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data. The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges. While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook. China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".

items.title: Revealed: African island fights offshore gambling network linked to UK family
items.summary: London-based property investors deny selling licences to casinos claiming to be based on Anjouan, a tiny Indian Ocean island The island of Anjouan, rising out of the Indian Ocean between Mozambique and Madagascar, is a corner of the Earth that few people have heard of, let alone…
items.body: The island of Anjouan, rising out of the Indian Ocean between Mozambique and Madagascar, is a corner of the Earth that few people have heard of, let alone laid eyes on. Known as Nzwani in the local language, this tiny volcanic island – one of a collection that make up the Union of Comoros – counts ylang-ylang oil and vanilla among its chief exports. Yet Anjouan has stumbled into a role at the heart of a much more dangerous but highly lucrative industry: underground online gambling. The African island has become notorious for selling licences to rogue casinos, many operating illegally. Some appear to be targeting vulnerable customers, while others have been accused of refusing to pay out winnings. At least one appears to be chasing British gamblers, via high-profile stunts involving the porn actor Bonnie Blue and the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson.

items.title: In pictures: More than 500,000 took to the streets as France protests erupted into violence
items.summary: Over 500,000 people took part in protests in France over the weekend, which became marred by violence, amid demonstrations against rising living costs.
items.body: Protests in France against rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people taking to the streets. Hundreds of thousands of people marched through various cities and protested peacefully but others set fire to the city hall in Limoges, gutting the 19th-century building. Lyon's city tourist office was also set ablaze, supermarkets were looted and there were attacks on police officers and vehicles and luxury boutiques, in what was described as the country's worst unrest in years. Officers used tear gas to restrain the crowds. One protester died of a heart attack, and another lost a hand. "Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday.

items.title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
items.summary: Trading standards officers say AI is "super-charging" existing scams through clones and fake websites.
items.body: Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams. Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot. If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say. AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards. For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist , external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using. Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.

items.title: The housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have become | Leilani Farha
items.summary: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power? Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing In the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada,…
items.body: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power? I n the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. He was living in a tent in the shadow of brand new skyscrapers, and had been homeless for about five years. At one point he swivelled around, pointed up at a crane on the skyline, and said: “Who are they building those for? Definitely not for me.” He was right. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy. Democracy promises that our living conditions are shaped by all of us, regardless of our station in life.

items.title: French unrest compounds debt crisis fears. Paris-listed stocks, bonds and the euro fall
items.summary: "It looks like either the bond markets riot, or the people riot, or both," one analyst told CNBC.
items.body: Social unrest , political instability and mounting national debt weighed on French assets on Monday, with government bonds and Paris-listed stocks under pressure. The euro was last seen down 0.15% against the U.S. dollar, and was 0.1% lower against the British pound. The French 10-year bond yield jumped more than 10 basis points, taking it just shy of its highest level in decades. Higher yields represent higher borrowing costs for the government in the debt market. The country's 2-year and 30-year yields were up 6 basis points and 8 basis points, respectively. Stocks are also feeling the heat, with the CAC 40 index down 1.7% in afternoon deals on Monday. The market has significantly underperformed its European peers in recent years as political volatility has mounted — despite only around 15% of its revenues being generated domestically — with banks under particular pressure.

items.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
items.summary: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.
items.body: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour. The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport. Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities. There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise". The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced. "We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone.

items.title: We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro Khanna
items.summary: Will California stand with the working class or the oligarchs in the vote this November? The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs? Proposition 40,…
items.body: Will California stand with the working class or the oligarchs in the vote this November? The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs? Proposition 40, California’s billionaire tax, is the most important ballot initiative in America and a fight for the soul of our party. Senator Bernie Sanders and I stand with the nurses and healthcare workers who put Prop 40 on the ballot. Governor Gavin Newsom stands with Peter Thiel, Sergey Brin and Elon Musk, Trump backers who all oppose it. Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Together they hold wealth equal to half of California’s economy. That wealth is up 20% this year alone. If they paid this tax, they would be worth the same as they were on Labor Day of this year .

items.title: Putin reportedly proposes three-way summit with Trump and Xi on Ukraine war — without Zelenskyy
items.summary: The report comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the United States, its largest military backer.
items.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table. The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.

items.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
items.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.
items.body: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China. Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market. A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy. The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.

items.title: Tourists are avoiding York, my home town – but I know how to get them back
items.summary: Are they put off by the hen parties, the tea rooms or the £5-an-hour parking? No matter. It’s time for my bold new approach ... York may be falling out of fashion with tourists. The BBC reports January-to-June visitor numbers to my home town fell 8% compared with 2025, with…
items.body: Are they put off by the hen parties, the tea rooms or the £5-an-hour parking? No matter. It’s time for my bold new approach ... York may be falling out of fashion with tourists. The BBC reports January-to-June visitor numbers to my home town fell 8% compared with 2025, with visits to city attractions down by 17%. This inspires a cocktail of conflicting emotions – selfish relief, a bit of huffiness (how dare they reject the birthplace of the Chocolate Orange and the KitKat?) and consternation. Slaloming through unpredictable, slow-moving tourist hordes in narrow medieval streets is far from my favourite activity (albeit probably good for my cognitive reserve), but tourists keep this city afloat. Our main economic activities in 2026 are “dressing up”, “tea and cake”, and “hen/stag night services (sub-categories: booze, kebabs, feather boas)”.

items.title: Saudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protection | Mohamad Bazzi
items.summary: After Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for help For years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince…
items.body: F or years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman , cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince understood the president’s transactional approach to power: he signed deals to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US weapons and invested billions more in American companies. Days after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Prince Mohammed pledged to expand investment and trade with the US by $600bn over four years. He later promised to increase that investment to nearly $1tn, although it wasn’t entirely clear how Saudi Arabia would manage to plough a sum close to the kingdom’s entire annual GDP into a foreign economy over a few years.

items.title: NYSE becomes latest exchange to extend options hours as appetite for around-the-clock trading grows
items.summary: The New York Stock Exchange becomes second major exchange to announce extended-hours options trading for heavily traded ETFs and single stocks, following CBOE.
items.body: The New York Stock Exchange becomes the second major exchange to announce extended-hours options trading for heavily-traded ETFs and single stocks, following CBOE's announcement that it will introduce extended trading for 25 single stocks and five ETFs. Extended options trading hours for the NYSE, which is owned and operated by the Intercontinental Exchange , begin Monday, and will operate from 7:30 AM to 9:25 AM ET, while the new late trading session will operate from 4:00 PM to 4:15 PM ET. Twenty-nine major stocks and funds are available for extended trading including Nvidia , Bank of America , the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF . Beginning Dec. 6, 2026, NYSE will extend trading to 23 hours, five days a week in those same names.

items.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
items.summary: Tech firm Nscale says it is still committed to building the site in Essex.
items.body: A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project. Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton , Essex. However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement. A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said. But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday , external , Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.

items.title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
items.summary: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its…
items.body: Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing. The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline. The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said. The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.

items.title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
items.summary: Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense.
items.body: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine . U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations. In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.

items.title: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
items.summary: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending. China’s GDP grew by 4.5%…
items.body: Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending. China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%. China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures. Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%. Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.

items.title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
items.summary: With $5 billion already deployed off its balance sheet, JPMorgan Chase is racing ahead on direct investments in defense tech, hardware and supply chains.
items.body: JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative , the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms. The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments , has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added.

items.summary: Charities in Hampshire tell the BBC that furniture poverty is becoming an increasing problem.
items.body: Charities say they are "busier than ever" helping people living in furniture poverty. BBC South spoke to people and organisations affected in Hampshire after national charity End Furniture Poverty said about six million in the UK were living without essentials such as beds, cookers and fridges. And a group of MPs is calling on the government to develop a national strategy to address the problem. They said they believed that a safe, secure and sustainable home should include access to the basic furniture necessary for everyday living. Among those who have needed help is Yana Osibchuk, who moved to the UK from Ukraine after the war began with her son, her dog and two suitcases - and was placed into social housing. "It was absolutely empty - no furniture, no cooker, no fridge, nothing and no flooring," she said.

items.title: Ellie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mine
items.summary: Singer ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land The singer Ellie Goulding has admitted her error at having promoted diamonds at the centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land in Australia, despite…
items.body: The singer Ellie Goulding has admitted her error at having promoted diamonds at the centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land in Australia, despite having spent years campaigning on environmental issues – including the effects of mining on ancestral lands. She appeared at a event in London earlier this month for the jewellery brand Boodles, modelling some of its newly acquired pink diamonds , some of which came from a controversial mine in Western Australia. “Protecting the environment is a cause close to my heart. I always strive to uphold those values. Regretfully, in this instance, I fell short,” said Goulding, who was made an MBE for services to biodiversity and the climate last year. “I was not aware of the concerns surrounding the Argyle mine and I am grateful that it has been brought to my attention.

items.title: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi rejects criticism around weak yen and high interest rates
items.summary: The prime minister denied that her policies were responsible for the yen’s weakness or rising JGB yields.
items.body: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has rejected criticism that she was on one hand responsible for a weak yen and on the other for pushing up interest rates in the country. Speaking in parliament, Takaichi said; "I have been repeatedly criticized for 'Takaichi's weak yen' and 'Takaichi's high interest rates,' but I clearly deny that," according to a Reuters translation of her remarks in Japanese. She was responding to a question from an opposition party lawmaker Yoshifumi Hamano, who asked about the compilation of a second supplementary budget for the country. Takaichi also said that her administration will increase confidence in the yen by building a strong economy.

As the war in the Middle East rattles the global economy, business leaders are pressing the chancellor for a package of emergency support to soften the impact from soaring fuel costs and energy bills. Healey has pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households and businesses “breathing space”.

A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson demanded action to improve air travel in response to numerous incidents in which passengers had been left stranded without assistance. The Department for Transport said airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month.

items.body: Brent crude oil prices neared recent highs Monday, as Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi Arabia and Ukraine struck oil facilities in Russia. Global benchmark Brent futures lost 31 cents to close at $109.55 per barrel after hitting $110.70 earlier. U.S. West Texas intermediate advanced $2.25 to close at $103.66 per barrel. Prices pulled back from session highs as traders weighed possibly higher Russian supplies hitting the market after U.S. sanctions relief on Friday. The Houthis claimed Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces. CNBC could not verify the Houthi claims. The Saudis have not issued a public statement confirming them.

items.body: The leftwing news site the Canary has announced that it is closing indefinitely. Earlier this year the media outlet was blocked from accessing funds and has faced allegations of internal turmoil . The outlet, founded in 2015 at the height of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn, said in a social media post it would be closing “for the foreseeable future”. The announcement also included allegations that the title had faced “malicious lies” by former employees. It said such claims had been part of “multiple attacks” it had faced which had made its situation “unsustainable, both financially and operationally”. In a statement, the Canary said: “After 11 years, we take this action with deep sadness and regret.

items.title: China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates
items.summary: China's economic growth accelerated in the third quarter, as foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset sluggish consumer demand.
items.body: China's economic growth accelerated to 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as robust foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset drags from a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand. Third-quarter growth beat Reuters-polled economists' expectation of a 4.4% expansion, and was also higher than the three-year low of 4.3% in the second quarter . "The rebound in September salvaged the lukewarm performance in July and August," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, attributing the recovery to improved government investment that helped arrest the consistent worsening in fixed asset investment, an "ever-strong" external sector and a weak base. China's monthly trade surplus reached a record high of $133.5 billion .

items.title: India protests and crackdowns hit festive season sales
items.body: NEW DELHI -- For years, Neetu and her son Nikhil have been hawking traditional Indian outfits at a street market near the iconic Jantar Mantar protest site in the heart of New Delhi. With the festive season having kicked off a little more than a week ago, their sales should be soaring; instead, the merchants are staring at huge losses.

items.title: ‘We’re living in darkness’: six years of scaffolding, still no post-Grenfell cladding
items.summary: Building safety regulator delays leave London tower block beset by security and vandalism problems It’s a sunny day with bright blue skies in north London, but you wouldn’t know that in Natasha Dyett’s flat. Most of the rooms are consumed in shadow, while her teenage son’s…
items.body: I t’s a sunny day with bright blue skies in north London , but you wouldn’t know that in Natasha Dyett’s flat. Most of the rooms are consumed in shadow, while her teenage son’s bedroom is almost completely dark, apart from a few slits of light coming through the window. She lives in Archway Heights, a nine-storey block of flats that has been covered in scaffolding for more than six years for cladding works that still haven’t started. The building’s residents say the scaffolding is making life a misery by blocking natural light from entering their homes, especially in places where metal sheets have almost entirely covered whole windows. Others are unable to open windows that have been obstructed by the wooden and metal structure outside. “It’s miserable, it’s like we’re living in darkness,” said Dyett, a 52-year-old market trader living on the third floor.

items.title: China's CXMT shares fall nearly 8% as investors look past chipmaker's profit turnaround
items.summary: CXMT shares fell nearly 8% on Monday after the company released its earnings forecast for the first nine months of 2026.
items.body: Shares of ChangXin Memory Technologies , or CXMT, closed 7.8% lower Monday, even as the company forecast a sharp swing to profitability for the first nine months of 2026. CXMT said in a filing Friday that it expects net profit attributable to shareholders of between 131 billion yuan ($19.58 billion) and 132.5 billion yuan for the January-to-September period, reversing a net loss of 5.28 billion yuan a year earlier, according to a Google translation of the filing. The company expects revenue of around 265 billion yuan to 270 billion yuan, an increase of 232.9 billion yuan to 237.9 billion yuan from the same period a year earlier. The company attributed the sharp improvement to rapidly growing demand for AI computing power since the second half of 2025, which has boosted the global DRAM market, leading to supply shortages and significant price increases, according to the filing.

items.title: Indian chemical firms turn to foreign partners to crack chip supply chains
items.body: BENGALURU -- A slew of Indian chemical companies have announced their entry into the semiconductor industry on the back of the country's multibillion-dollar chip supply chain push. But meeting the exacting standards of chip fabrication plants requires purification technology and access to customers that Indian businesses don't have, pushing some to turn to foreign partnerships.
